questions.q: Which cardinal sign of acute inflammation, described by Celsus, is directly caused by arteriolar vasodilation and increased blood flow to the injured area?
questions.explain: Rubor (redness) and calor (heat) result from arteriolar vasodilation and increased local blood flow. Tumor (swelling) results from exudation of fluid and cells, while dolor (pain) is caused by mediators like bradykinin and prostaglandins.

open.q: Name the Latin cardinal sign of acute inflammation characterized by redness resulting from arteriolar vasodilation.

questions.q: What is the most common mechanism responsible for increased vascular permeability during the immediate transient response of acute inflammation?
options: Direct necrosis of arteriolar smooth muscle
Contraction of endothelial cells in postcapillary venules
questions.explain: Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotrienes bind endothelial receptors in postcapillary venules, inducing actin-myosin contraction and widening intercellular endothelial gaps within minutes.

open.q: What endothelial cellular mechanism accounts for the immediate transient increase in vascular permeability in postcapillary venules during acute inflammation?

questions.q: How does an inflammatory exudate differ biochemically and physically from a transudate?
options: An exudate has high protein content and specific gravity above 1.020
An exudate has low protein content and results purely from elevated hydrostatic pressure
An exudate is acellular with specific gravity below 1.012
An exudate forms exclusively due to hypoalbuminaemia
questions.explain: An exudate leaks through hyperpermeable inflamed vessels and is rich in plasma proteins (fibrinogen, immunoglobulins) and leukocytes with specific gravity > 1.020, whereas a transudate is an ultrafiltrate of plasma with low protein and specific gravity < 1.012.

open.q: How does an inflammatory exudate differ from a transudate in terms of protein concentration and specific gravity?
accept: High protein content and specific gravity above 1.020
Protein-rich with specific gravity greater than 1.020

questions.q: Which family of adhesion molecules mediates the initial low-affinity rolling of leukocytes along the vascular endothelium during acute inflammation?
questions.explain: E-selectin, P-selectin, and L-selectin bind sialyl-Lewis X-modified glycoproteins on leukocytes and endothelium to mediate weak, transient tethering and rolling before firm integrin-mediated arrest.

open.q: Name the family of cell adhesion molecules responsible for the initial rolling of leukocytes along activated vascular endothelium.

questions.q: A 6-month-old boy presents with recurrent severe bacterial skin and mucosal infections without pus formation and delayed separation of the umbilical cord. Flow cytometry shows absent CD18 on neutrophils. Which step of leukocyte recruitment is primarily defective?
options: Margination in the central axial stream
questions.explain: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1) is caused by mutations in the common beta-2 integrin subunit (CD18), impairing LFA-1 and Mac-1 binding to endothelial ICAM-1 and preventing firm leukocyte arrest and transmigration.

open.q: In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 caused by CD18 beta-2 integrin deficiency, which step of leukocyte extravasation fails?

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin-superfamily molecule expressed at intercellular endothelial junctions facilitates leukocyte transmigration (diapedesis) across the vessel wall?
questions.explain: Platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1 or CD31) is expressed on both leukocytes and endothelial intercellular junctions, guiding leukocytes through the interendothelial cleft during diapedesis.

open.q: Name the endothelial junction adhesion molecule that guides leukocytes through interendothelial spaces during transmigration (diapedesis).

questions.q: Which complement fragment acts as both a potent endogenous chemoattractant for neutrophils and an activator of leukocyte integrin avidity?
questions.explain: C5a is a powerful chemotactic factor and anaphylatoxin that attracts neutrophils and monocytes and activates leukocyte integrins, whereas C3b functions primarily as an opsonin.

open.q: Name the complement cleavage fragment that acts as a potent neutrophil chemoattractant and anaphylatoxin during acute inflammation.

questions.q: Which complement fragment coats microbial surfaces to promote recognition and engulfment by neutrophil and macrophage complement receptors (opsonization)?
questions.explain: C3b and its inactive cleavage fragment iC3b covalently bind microbial cell walls and act as major opsonins recognized by phagocyte CR1 and CR3 receptors, alongside IgG Fc fragments.

open.q: Name the major complement-derived opsonin that coats bacteria to enhance phagocytosis.

questions.q: Inside the phagolysosome of activated neutrophils, which enzyme converts hydrogen peroxide and chloride ions into the potent microbicidal oxidant hypochlorous acid (HOCl)?
questions.explain: Azurophilic granules deliver myeloperoxidase (MPO) into the phagolysosome, where MPO catalyzes the reaction of H2O2 with Cl- to generate hypochlorous acid (bleach), the most bactericidal agent in neutrophils.

open.q: Name the neutrophil azurophilic granule enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide and chloride ions into microbicidal hypochlorous acid.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with recurrent catalase-positive bacterial and fungal abscesses including Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species. Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) dye reduction test is completely negative. Which enzyme complex is defective?
questions.explain: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by inherited defects in components of phagocyte NADPH oxidase (phox), abolishing the respiratory burst and superoxide generation; patients are vulnerable to catalase-positive organisms that degrade their own H2O2.

open.q: Which phagocyte enzyme complex is defective in chronic granulomatous disease, resulting in a negative nitroblue tetrazolium test and recurrent catalase-positive infections?

questions.q: Which cell type serves as the richest tissue source of preformed histamine granules released immediately upon physical trauma, C3a/C5a binding, or IgE cross-linking?
questions.explain: Perivascular mast cells store abundant preformed histamine in cytoplasmic granules and degranulate immediately in response to injury, anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a), or allergen-mediated IgE cross-linking.

open.q: Name the perivascular tissue resident cell type that serves as the major source of preformed histamine granules in early acute inflammation.

questions.q: Which enzyme liberates arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids to initiate eicosanoid synthesis?
questions.explain: Phospholipase A2 is activated by mechanical, chemical, or inflammatory stimuli (and inhibited by corticosteroids) to cleave arachidonic acid from plasma membrane phospholipids.

open.q: Name the membrane enzyme inhibited by corticosteroids that cleaves arachidonic acid from cellular phospholipids.

questions.q: Which arachidonic acid metabolite generated via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, whereas cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) cause intense bronchospasm and vasoconstriction?
questions.explain: 5-Lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid to 5-HPETE and LTA4, which is hydrolyzed to LTB4 (a potent chemotactic agent for neutrophils) or conjugated with glutathione to form LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4.

open.q: Name the 5-lipoxygenase-derived arachidonic acid metabolite that acts as a potent chemoattractant and activator for neutrophils.

questions.q: Which class of arachidonic acid derivatives, synthesized through transcellular biosynthetic cooperation between neutrophils and platelets, actively inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis and promotes resolution of acute inflammation?
questions.explain: Lipoxins (LXA4 and LXB4) are specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators produced late in acute inflammation that block leukocyte recruitment and stimulate macrophage clearance of apoptotic neutrophils.

open.q: Name the specialized pro-resolving arachidonic acid metabolites produced by transcellular biosynthesis that inhibit neutrophil recruitment and promote resolution of inflammation.

questions.q: Activation of Hageman factor (Factor XII) on negatively charged surfaces simultaneously triggers the coagulation cascade, fibrinolytic system, complement system, and which vasoactive peptide system?
questions.explain: Activated Factor XIIa converts prekallikrein to kallikrein, which cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to release bradykinin, a potent mediator of vascular permeability, vasodilation, and pain.

open.q: Name the plasma protein mediator system activated by Factor XIIa that generates bradykinin.

questions.q: Which two pro-inflammatory cytokines act on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre via prostaglandin E2 induction to produce fever during infection and tissue injury?
questions.explain: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumour necrosis factor (TNF), along with IL-6, act as endogenous pyrogens that stimulate cyclooxygenase-2 in hypothalamic vascular endothelium to synthesize PGE2, raising the thermal set point.

open.q: Name two major endogenous pyrogenic cytokines that induce fever by stimulating hypothalamic prostaglandin E2 synthesis.

questions.q: Which morphologic pattern of acute inflammation is characterized by extensive exudation of fibrinogen that polymerizes into an eosinophilic meshwork on serosal surfaces such as the pericardium or pleura?
questions.explain: Fibrinous exudates develop when large vascular leaks allow high-molecular-weight fibrinogen to pass into body cavities (e.g., rheumatic pericarditis, giving a bread-and-butter appearance) and may resolve by fibrinolysis or organize into fibrous adhesions.

open.q: Name the morphologic pattern of acute inflammation seen in uraemic or rheumatic pericarditis characterized by dense exudation of fibrinogen onto serosal surfaces.

questions.q: A localized collection of pus composed of necrotic tissue debris, viable and dead neutrophils, and oedema fluid walled off by granulation tissue and fibrosis is termed what?
questions.explain: An abscess is a focal suppurative (purulent) inflammatory lesion typically caused by pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, featuring a central zone of liquefactive necrosis surrounded by preserved neutrophils and dilated vessels.

open.q: Name a localized, walled-off collection of pus within a tissue or organ resulting from acute suppurative inflammation.

questions.q: Which mononuclear leukocyte is the dominant cellular orchestrator of chronic inflammation, capable of secreting both tissue-destructive enzymes and fibrogenic growth factors?
questions.explain: Tissue macrophages derived from circulating blood monocytes are the hallmark effector cells of chronic inflammation; classical (M1) macrophages promote microbicidal inflammation while alternative (M2) macrophages drive tissue repair and fibrosis.

open.q: Name the dominant mononuclear phagocyte that orchestrates tissue destruction and fibrosis in chronic inflammation.

questions.q: Which cytokine, secreted principally by Th1 lymphocytes and natural killer cells, is the primary activator of classical M1 macrophages and drives epithelioid cell transformation in granulomas?
questions.explain: IFN-gamma binds macrophage surface receptors to upregulate MHC class II expression, nitric oxide and ROS production, and fusion of activated epithelioid macrophages into multinucleated giant cells.

open.q: Name the Th1-derived cytokine that serves as the principal classical activator of macrophages and drives granuloma formation.

questions.q: What is the defining histological cellular aggregate of a granuloma?
options: A microscopic collection of activated epithelioid macrophages surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes
A sheet of polymorphonuclear neutrophils surrounding a central venule
A cluster of proliferating fibroblasts embedded in pure hyaline cartilage
An accumulation of eosinophils and mast cells around a dilated lymphatic
questions.explain: A granuloma is a focal chronic inflammatory reaction consisting of aggregated activated macrophages that acquire abundant pink cytoplasm resembling squamous epithelial cells (epithelioid cells), often accompanied by multinucleated giant cells and a peripheral collar of T lymphocytes.

open.q: What is the defining microscopic cellular composition of a granuloma?
accept: Aggregates of activated epithelioid macrophages surrounded by lymphocytes
Collection of epithelioid macrophages and lymphocytes

questions.q: In a Langhans multinucleated giant cell, how are the multiple nuclei characteristically arranged within the cytoplasm?
options: In a peripheral horseshoe or ring-like pattern
Randomly scattered throughout the entire cytoplasm
Packed tightly in a single central cluster
Aligned strictly in a single linear row across the centre
questions.explain: Langhans giant cells, characteristically seen in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis, display 20 or more nuclei arranged around the periphery of the cell in a horseshoe or ring configuration, whereas foreign-body giant cells have haphazardly scattered nuclei.

open.q: How are the nuclei characteristically arranged inside a Langhans multinucleated giant cell?
accept: Arranged at the periphery in a horseshoe or ring
Horseshoe arrangement at the cell periphery

questions.q: According to proliferative capacity, hepatocytes and renal proximal tubular epithelial cells belong to which tissue category?
questions.explain: Stable tissues reside in the G0 phase of the cell cycle with minimal baseline replication, but rapidly re-enter G1 to regenerate following parenchymal loss (such as partial hepatectomy) provided the extracellular matrix scaffold remains intact.

open.q: To which proliferative tissue category do hepatocytes and renal tubular epithelial cells belong?

questions.q: Why does acute viral hepatitis with hepatocellular necrosis typically heal by complete parenchymal regeneration, whereas chronic hepatitis with collapse of the reticulin framework progresses to cirrhosis?
options: Regeneration requires an intact extracellular matrix basement membrane scaffold
Hepatocytes are permanent cells that cannot divide after childhood
Viral hepatitis inhibits all hepatic vascular endothelial growth factor
Kupffer cells secrete collagenase that destroys healthy hepatocytes
questions.explain: Even in tissues with high regenerative capacity like the liver, orderly restoration of normal architecture requires preservation of the underlying extracellular matrix and reticulin scaffold; architectural collapse leads to scar deposition instead.

open.q: What structural prerequisite must remain intact for stable parenchymal cells like hepatocytes to regenerate normal tissue architecture rather than forming a scar?
accept: Intact basement membrane and reticulin framework

questions.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
questions.q: Which pink, soft, granular tissue appears within 3 to 5 days of injury as the histological hallmark of healing, composed of proliferating fibroblasts and newly formed leaky capillaries?
questions.explain: Granulation tissue represents the early vascularized connective tissue scaffold of wound repair, characterized microscopically by numerous thin-walled newly formed capillaries (angiogenesis) and plump myofibroblasts in a loose edematous matrix.

open.q: Name the specialized vascularized repair tissue composed of proliferating fibroblasts and newly formed capillaries that appears 3 to 5 days after injury.

questions.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
questions.q: Which growth factor is the single most potent inducer of angiogenesis during wound repair and tumour growth by stimulating endothelial cell migration and proliferation?
questions.explain: VEGF (particularly VEGF-A), strongly induced by tissue hypoxia via HIF-1 alpha, stimulates endothelial tip cell sprouting, migration, proliferation, and capillary lumen formation.

open.q: Name the principal growth factor that drives angiogenesis by stimulating vascular endothelial cell migration and proliferation.

questions.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
questions.q: Which fibrogenic cytokine is the most potent stimulator of fibroblast collagen synthesis and inhibits matrix metalloproteinases during scar formation?
questions.explain: TGF-beta promotes fibroblast migration and proliferation, upregulates transcription of collagen and fibronectin genes, and decreases extracellular matrix degradation by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).

open.q: Name the key fibrogenic growth factor that stimulates collagen synthesis by fibroblasts and inhibits matrix metalloproteinases during scar formation.

questions.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
questions.q: During skin wound healing by secondary intention, which specialized contractile cells express alpha-smooth muscle actin and pull the wound edges together to reduce defect size?
questions.explain: Myofibroblasts possess ultrastructural and functional features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, generating strong contractile forces that close large open wounds by secondary intention.

open.q: Name the specialized contractile cells containing smooth muscle actin that mediate wound contraction during healing by secondary intention.

questions.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
questions.q: During wound maturation, provisional type III collagen deposited early in granulation tissue is degraded by matrix metalloproteinases and replaced by which stronger fibrillar collagen?
questions.explain: Early granulation tissue contains abundant pliable type III collagen, which is progressively remodeled into dense, cross-linked type I collagen to increase wound tensile strength up to 70–80% of unwounded skin.

open.q: Which fibrillar collagen type replaces early type III collagen during wound remodeling to provide maximum tensile strength to a mature scar?

questions.q: A 23-year-old Nigerian woman develops a firm, raised, lobulated fibrous nodule on her earlobe 6 months after ear piercing that extends well beyond the margins of the original puncture wound and recurs after simple surgical excision. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: A keloid is an exuberant accumulation of thick, hyalinized eosinophilic collagen bundles that grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound, shows genetic predisposition in individuals of African descent, and frequently recurs after excision—unlike a hypertrophic scar, which stays confined to the original wound borders and tends to regress.

open.q: Name the exuberant fibrous scar that grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and frequently recurs after excision.
